questions.q: For a fixed generator, what is the best discriminator at a point x?
options: D*(x) = p_data(x) / ( p_data(x) + p_g(x) )
D*(x) = p_g(x) / ( p_data(x) + p_g(x) )
D*(x) = 1/2 at every x, whatever the generator
D*(x) = p_data(x) − p_g(x)
questions.why: Proposition 1 of Goodfellow et al.: at each x the function a·log y + b·log(1−y) peaks at y = a/(a+b), with a = p_data(x) and b = p_g(x). In the lab no random nudge of this discriminator scored higher.

questions.q: What is the best value the generator can reach against a best-playing discriminator, and when?
options: −log 4, and only when p_g equals p_data
−log 2, whenever the discriminator outputs 1/2
+log 4, whenever the discriminator is fooled
There is no best value, because the generator can always score lower
questions.answer: −log 4, and only when p_g equals p_data
questions.why: max over D of V is −log 4 + 2·JSD(p_data ‖ p_g), and JSD is zero only for equal distributions. The lab row for the data itself prints −1.386294, which is −log 4.

questions.q: In the lab a confident discriminator (mean D(G(z)) = 0.0154) judges the same samples under two generator losses. What happens to the generator's gradient norm?
options: It is 0.4386 with log(1 − D) and 13.0146 with −log D, about 30 times larger
It is the same for both losses, because both have the same fixed point
It is 13.0146 with log(1 − D) and 0.4386 with −log D
It is zero for both losses once the discriminator is confident
questions.answer: It is 0.4386 with log(1 − D) and 13.0146 with −log D, about 30 times larger
questions.why: With respect to the logit, the gradient of log(1−D) has size D, which is near 0 here, and that of −log D has size 1−D, near 1. The paper says the two losses share a fixed point but the second gives much stronger gradients early in learning.

questions.q: All four lab seeds ended with discriminator accuracy between 0.461 and 0.515. What does the lab conclude from that?
options: Chance accuracy is not proof of a good generator: W1 was still 7 to 21 times the 0.016 floor
The generators match the data exactly, because the discriminator cannot tell them apart
The discriminators failed to train, so the runs say nothing about the generators
An accuracy below 0.5 means the generator is better than the real data
questions.answer: Chance accuracy is not proof of a good generator: W1 was still 7 to 21 times the 0.016 floor
questions.why: W1 to the data ran from 0.113 to 0.338 while two real samples differ by 0.016. A small discriminator trained for 2000 steps may not see what is left.

questions.q: How do Rombach et al. train the autoencoder that their latent diffusion models rely on?
options: With a perceptual loss and a patch-based adversarial objective
With a diffusion loss on the pixels
With a CLIP contrastive loss
With a causal mask and next-pixel prediction
questions.answer: With a perceptual loss and a patch-based adversarial objective
questions.why: Section 3.1 and appendix G of the latent diffusion paper. The patch-based discriminator exists only during that training, which is how a GAN idea ends up inside the VAE you run in ComfyUI.

questions.q: Your upscaler draws crisp lettering that was not readable in the source. What is the most likely cause?
options: An adversarial loss rewards what looks real, not what was there
The tiles overlapped too much
The model file is damaged
The upscaler ran in fp8
questions.answer: An adversarial loss rewards what looks real, not what was there
questions.why: The ESRGAN abstract speaks of hallucinated details. The loss has no way to know what was really in the picture.
